options.option_text: Heights (tall buildings, cliffs)
Open spaces (agoraphobia)
Closed spaces (claustrophobia)
Darkness (nyctophobia) too

questions.explanation: ACROPHOBIA — Greek 'akron' = peak, 'phobos' = fear. FEAR OF HEIGHTS. Common phobia (~5% of population). Symptoms: dizziness, sweating, panic when on tall building, balcony, cliff. ROOT 'acro' also in: ACROBAT (one who walks on heights), ACROPOLIS ('high city' — the citadel of ancient Athens), ACRONYM (top of words). PHOBIA SUFFIX: from Greek god PHOBOS (fear), brother of DEIMOS (terror). MASTER LIST OF PHOBIAS to learn (PYQ favourites): ACRO (heights), AGORA (open spaces), CLAUSTRO (closed spaces), HYDRO (water), PYRO (fire), NYCTO (darkness), THANATO (death), HEMO (blood), ARACHNO (spiders), OPHIDIO (snakes), CYNO (dogs), ZOO (animals), XENO (foreigners), GLOSSO (public speaking), TRISKAIDEKA (number 13).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: XENOPHOBIA is the fear / hatred of:

options.option_text: Foreigners or strangers
Snakes (ophidiophobia)
Tight spaces (claustrophobia)
Number 13 (triskaidekaphobia)

questions.explanation: XENOPHOBIA — Greek 'xenos' = stranger / foreigner. Fear or hatred of foreigners / strangers / what is foreign. SOCIAL/POLITICAL phenomenon as much as personal phobia — anti-immigrant sentiment, racism. Same root: XENON (a noble gas — discovered + named because it's 'strange/foreign'), XENOGRAFT (transplant from one species to another), XENIAL (relating to hospitality, Greek custom toward strangers). RELATED phobias: ETHNOPHOBIA (fear of certain ethnic groups), HOMOPHOBIA (fear / prejudice against gay people — 'homos' = same; also 'homo' = same in homosexual). Greek roots are ESSENTIAL for English vocabulary; ~25% of English words trace to Greek roots.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: HYDROPHOBIA is fear of WATER. It is also a CLINICAL SIGN of which disease?

options.option_text: Rabies (dog bite — viral disease)
Tuberculosis (lung infection)
Malaria (mosquito-borne)
Tetanus (lockjaw) too alone

questions.explanation: HYDROPHOBIA — fear of water. CLASSIC SYMPTOM of LATE-STAGE RABIES (caused by Lyssavirus, transmitted by infected animal bites — dogs primarily, also bats, monkeys, foxes). Patient unable to drink water due to painful throat spasms triggered by sight/sound of water. Once symptoms appear, rabies is almost 100% FATAL (no cure). PREVENTION: post-exposure VACCINATION (within hours/days of bite). India has world's highest rabies deaths (~36% of global deaths). Govt's STREET DOG vaccination + 'CARE OF STRAY' programs ongoing. INSIGHT — Louis Pasteur developed first rabies vaccine 1885 (saved 9-yr-old Joseph Meister, bitten by rabid dog). Pasteur Institute in India = primary rabies-vaccine producer; centres at Coonoor, Pune, Kolkata.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: Public speaking (most common phobia)
Animals (zoophobia is the term)
Books (bibliophobia is the term)
Crowds (enochlophobia is the term)

questions.explanation: GLOSSOPHOBIA — Greek 'glossa' = tongue. Fear of PUBLIC SPEAKING. World's MOST COMMON phobia (~75% of people experience some level). Often topped Jerry Seinfeld's joke: 'people fear public speaking more than death — at a funeral, you'd rather be in the casket than giving the eulogy.' Same root: POLYGLOT (knows many languages), GLOSSARY (list of language words), GLOSSITIS (inflamed tongue), HIEROGLYPHICS (sacred writing). RELATED phobias: TROPHOPHOBIA (fear of trophies — anxiety about success!); ATYCHIPHOBIA (fear of failure); SOCIAL anxiety disorder = broader umbrella. TREATMENT: cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), graded exposure, public-speaking clubs (Toastmasters), beta-blockers for performance anxiety.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: TRISKAIDEKAPHOBIA is the unusual fear of:

options.option_text: Number 13 (deeply rooted superstition)
Triangles (geometric shape) too
Three things together (option here)
Tridents (3-pronged spear) too

questions.explanation: TRISKAIDEKAPHOBIA — Greek 'tris' (three) + 'kai' (and) + 'deka' (ten) = thirteen + 'phobia'. Fear / superstition around number 13. Many buildings skip floor 13 (go from 12 to 14). FRIDAY THE 13TH is considered unlucky in Western culture (subject of Hollywood horror franchise). Origin: possibly Last Supper (13 attended; Judas Iscariot = 13th, betrayed Jesus); or Norse mythology (Loki = 13th god, caused Balder's death). PARASKEVIDEKATRIAPHOBIA = fear specifically of Friday the 13th. INDIAN SUPERSTITION: avoid number 7 in some contexts (Saturday = Shani); 8 in others. ALSO EXAM-WORTHY phobias: COULROPHOBIA (clowns), TRYPOPHOBIA (clusters of holes), NOMOPHOBIA (fear of being WITHOUT MOBILE phone — modern!), PHILOPHOBIA (fear of love).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: Spiders (creepy 8-legged arthropods)
Snakes (ophidiophobia is the term)
Insects in general (entomophobia)
Bees (apiphobia or melissophobia)

questions.explanation: ARACHNOPHOBIA — Greek 'arachne' = spider. Fear of spiders. ORIGIN of name: GREEK MYTH — Arachne, a mortal weaver, challenged goddess Athena to weaving contest, won; Athena turned her into a spider in punishment (or out of pity). Hence ARACHNIDS = class including spiders, scorpions, ticks, mites (8 legs). Spiders can be deadly (Black Widow, Brown Recluse, Sydney Funnel-Web), but most are harmless to humans. India has Trapdoor spiders, scorpions; check shoe before wearing in rural areas. Common: ENTOMOPHOBIA (insects); MUSOPHOBIA (mice); CYNOPHOBIA (dogs); AILUROPHOBIA (cats); OPHIDIOPHOBIA (snakes); APHENPHOSMPHOBIA (touch).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: NOMOPHOBIA, a modern phobia, is the fear of:

options.option_text: Being WITHOUT a mobile phone (No-Mobile-Phobia)
Following social rules (nomos = law)
Foreign cultures (general phobia) too
Reading books (a different phobia)

questions.explanation: NOMOPHOBIA — coined 2008 in UK study; from 'NO MObile PHone phobia'. Fear of being without mobile phone / unable to use it. Symptoms: anxiety when phone battery dies, no signal, left phone at home. ~70% of smartphone users show signs. SAME ERA: FOMO ('Fear Of Missing Out' — anxiety about events / news on social media missed); SCREEN ADDICTION; PHANTOM POCKET VIBRATION. Modern phobias also: SELFITIS (compulsive selfie-taking — APA recognised); TECHNOPHOBIA (fear of technology). PHILOSOPHICAL angle — these aren't classical phobias but reflect modern anxieties tied to tech dependence. Cures: digital detox, screen-time limits, mindfulness. INDIA: highest mobile-phone usage globally; ~700 million smartphone users.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: A person diagnosed with CLAUSTROPHOBIA would experience intense anxiety in which of the following situations?

options.option_text: standing alone in a vast open field at midday
riding in a small, crowded elevator with no windows
speaking to a large audience in an open auditorium
walking through a busy street market during daytime

questions.explanation: CLAUSTROPHOBIA is the fear of confined or enclosed spaces (Latin 'claustrum' = enclosed place + Greek 'phobia'). A small, windowless elevator is a classic trigger. Option A is the opposite condition — agoraphobia. Options C and D involve social or public exposure, not confinement.

questions.stem: NYCTOPHOBIA takes its root from the Greek word 'nyx'. What does this phobia specifically involve?

options.option_text: intense dread of loud noises and sudden sharp sounds
irrational fear of darkness or the absence of light
persistent anxiety around enclosed and windowless rooms
fear of open, unpopulated outdoor spaces after sunset

questions.explanation: In Greek mythology, 'Nyx' is the goddess of night; 'nyx/nyktos' means night or darkness. NYCTOPHOBIA is therefore the irrational fear of darkness. Option D is a tempting trap — nyctophobia is about darkness itself, not open spaces at night (that blends agoraphobia). Option A describes phonophobia; Option C describes claustrophobia.

questions.stem: Clinically, AGORAPHOBIA is best defined as the fear of situations where:

options.option_text: crowds gather in confined indoor environments like malls
escape might be difficult or help unavailable if needed
unfamiliar strangers could initiate unwanted social contact
wide open landscapes produce a sense of spatial disorientation

questions.explanation: Though 'agora' means marketplace, the DSM clinical definition of agoraphobia is fear of any situation where escape would be difficult or help unavailable during a panic attack — not merely open spaces. Option D (open landscapes) reflects the popular misconception. Option A (crowded indoors) is close but incomplete. Option C describes social anxiety disorder, not agoraphobia.

questions.stem: An employee who persistently refuses to use computers, avoids all digital devices, and panics around new technology is exhibiting signs of:

options.option_text: Ergophobia — deep-rooted aversion to any form of work
Technophobia — irrational fear of or hostility toward technology
Xenophobia — discomfort and distrust toward unfamiliar things
Logophobia — anxiety triggered by words or verbal interaction

questions.explanation: TECHNOPHOBIA (Greek 'technē' = skill/craft + 'phobos' = fear) denotes fear of or resistance to advanced technology. Option C (xenophobia) is a trap since technology can feel 'foreign', but xenophobia specifically targets people or cultures. Ergophobia concerns work broadly, not technology. Logophobia concerns words and verbal expression.

questions.stem: The suffix '-phobia' is derived from PHOBOS in Greek mythology. Which statement correctly identifies Phobos?

options.option_text: the god of darkness and ruler of the underworld domain
the personification of fear, son of Ares the war-god
the twin deity of Deimos who embodied panic in battle
the deity of night and prophetic dreams during sleep

questions.explanation: Phobos (fear) and Deimos (dread/panic) are twin sons of Ares and Aphrodite. Option C is a near-miss: Phobos and Deimos are siblings, but Deimos — not Phobos — specifically personifies panic and battlefield terror. Option A describes Hades; Option D describes Nyx or Morpheus. Both moons of Mars are named Phobos and Deimos after these figures.

questions.stem: ERGOPHOBIA, if untreated, would most directly interfere with a person's ability to:

options.option_text: board a commercial aircraft for an overseas assignment
sustain regular employment or complete assigned duties
deliver a prepared speech before a professional audience
enter a densely crowded shopping complex or marketplace

questions.explanation: ERGOPHOBIA derives from Greek 'ergon' (work) + 'phobia'; it is an irrational fear of work or the workplace. The root 'ergon' also appears in 'ergonomics', 'energy', and 'synergy'. Option C is a trap — it describes glossophobia (public speaking). Option A relates to aerophobia (flight). Option D relates to agoraphobia or ochlophobia (crowds). Only B directly targets the fear of work itself.

questions.stem: TAPHOPHOBIA, which reached documented peak prevalence in 18th–19th century Europe, is defined as the morbid fear of:

options.option_text: being struck by lightning during an outdoor thunderstorm
being interred alive while still in a living state
contracting a terminal disease with no available cure
permanent abandonment in a remote and uninhabited place

questions.explanation: TAPHOPHOBIA comes from Greek 'taphos' (grave/burial) + 'phobia'. Before modern death-certification, premature burial was a real documented occurrence in Europe, driving widespread taphophobia. Edgar Allan Poe's 'The Premature Burial' reflects this anxiety. The root 'taphos' also appears in 'epitaph' (inscription on a grave). Option C describes nosophobia; Option A describes astraphobia or keraunophobia.
